Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have a complete solution.  
The set of admissible numbers of sunny lines is  

\[
\boxed{\begin{cases}
\{0,1\}, & n=3\text{ or }n=4,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,\dots ,n-2\}, & n\ge 5 .
\end{cases}}
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Geometry of the required points.**  
   \[
   \mathcal P_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\mid a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\}
   \]
   is the set of lattice points in the right‑angled triangle with vertices
   \((1,1),(n,1),(1,n)\).  
   For each \(i\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) define the *column*
   \[
   C_i=\{(i,b)\mid 1\le b\le n+1-i\},
   \qquad |C_i|=n+1-i .
   \]
   The columns are disjoint and \(\displaystyle\mathcal P_n=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}C_i\).

2. **Upper bound for the number of sunny lines.**  
   *Lemma 1.* A sunny line meets each column \(C_i\) in **at most one** point
   (otherwise it would be vertical).  
   Hence a sunny line can contain at most \(n\) points of \(\mathcal P_n\).  

   Let a configuration contain \(k\) sunny lines and \(m=n-k\) non‑sunny
   lines.  Every non‑sunny line can be taken vertical, because a vertical line
   is the only non‑sunny line that can contain more than one point of a column.
   To maximise the number of points covered by the \(m\) vertical lines we let
   them be the columns with the largest cardinalities, i.e. \(C_1,\dots ,C_m\).
   Consequently the total number of points that can be covered by the whole
   configuration is at most  

   \[
   k\cdot n+\sum_{i=1}^{m}|C_i|
   =k n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}(n+1-i).
   \tag{1}
   \]

   The set \(\mathcal P_n\) contains  

   \[
   |\mathcal P_n|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(n+1-i)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}
   \tag{2}
   \]
   points.  Since every point must be covered, (1) must be at least (2):
   \[
   \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\le k n+\frac{(n-k)(n+k+1)}{2}.
   \]

   After elementary simplification this inequality becomes  

   \[
   k\le n-2 .
   \tag{3}
   \]

   For \(n=3,4\) the right‑hand side of (3) equals \(1\); for \(n\ge5\) it equals
   \(n-2\).  Thus no configuration can have more than the numbers of sunny
   lines stated in the answer.

3. **Construction attaining every admissible \(k\).**  

   *Base family.*  For each \(i=1,\dots ,n\) take the vertical line  

   \[
   L_i:\;x=i .
   \]

   These \(n\) lines cover all points of \(\mathcal P_n\).

   *Introducing sunny lines.*  The columns that consist of a single point are
   \(C_n=\{(n,1)\}\) and, when \(n\ge5\), also \(C_{n-1}=\{(n-1,2)\}\).
   Choose any \(k\) of these columns (possible exactly when \(k\) satisfies (3)).
   For each chosen column \(C_i\) delete the vertical line \(L_i\) and insert the
   sunny line  

   \[
   S_i:\; y-(n+1-i)=\frac12\bigl(x-i\bigr),
   \qquad\text{slope } \tfrac12\neq0,\infty,-1 .
   \]

   The line \(S_i\) meets the integer lattice inside the triangle only at the
   unique point \((i,n+1-i)\); therefore it is sunny and covers precisely the
   point of the replaced column.

   After performing the replacement for the chosen \(k\) columns we have:
   * exactly \(k\) sunny lines (\(S_i\));
   * the remaining \(n-k\) vertical lines still cover all points of the other
     columns;
   * the total number of lines stays \(n\).

   Hence every integer \(k\) that satisfies (3) is attainable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Detailed Solution**

### 1.  The required set of points  

For a fixed integer \(n\ge 3\) define  

\[
\mathcal P_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^{2}\mid a\ge1,\;b\ge1,\;a+b\le n+1\}.
\]

Geometrically \(\mathcal P_n\) is the set of lattice points inside the right‑
angled triangle with vertices \((1,1),(n,1),(1,n)\).

For each \(i\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) let  

\[
C_i=\{(i,b)\mid 1\le b\le n+1-i\}.
\]

The columns \(C_1,\dots ,C_n\) are pairwise disjoint, \(|C_i|=n+1-i\), and  

\[
\mathcal P_n=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}C_i .
\tag{4}
\]

Consequently  

\[
|\mathcal P_n|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(n+1-i)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
\tag{5}
\]

A line is **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0\) (horizontal),
\(\infty\) (vertical) and \(-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Upper bound for the number of sunny lines  

Let a family \(\mathcal L=\{L_1,\dots ,L_n\}\) of \(n\) distinct lines cover
\(\mathcal P_n\).  Denote by  

\[
k:=|\{L_i\in\mathcal L\mid L_i\text{ is sunny}\}|
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
m:=n-k
\]

the numbers of sunny and non‑sunny lines, respectively.

#### Lemma 2.1  
A sunny line meets each column \(C_i\) in at most one point.

*Proof.*  If a line contained two distinct points of the same column, those
points would have the same abscissa, forcing the line to be vertical, which is
not sunny. ∎

Hence a sunny line can contain at most one point from each of the \(n\) columns,
i.e. at most \(n\) points of \(\mathcal P_n\).

To maximise the total number of points that can be covered by the \(m\) non‑sunny
lines we may assume that every non‑sunny line is vertical (any other orientation
covers at most one point of a column, so replacing it by a vertical line can
only increase the number of points it covers).  A vertical line can cover the
whole column on which it lies.  Therefore the most points that can be covered
by the \(m\) non‑sunny lines is obtained by taking the \(m\) columns of largest
size, namely \(C_1,\dots ,C_m\).  Their total size is  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}|C_i|=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(n+1-i)
=\frac{m\,(2n+2-(m+1))}{2}
=\frac{(n-k)(n+k+1)}{2}.
\tag{6}
\]

Together with the at‑most‑\(n\) points per sunny line we obtain the inequality  

\[
|\mathcal P_n|
\le k\cdot n+\frac{(n-k)(n+k+1)}{2}.
\tag{7}
\]

Using (5) for \(|\mathcal P_n|\) and simplifying (7) gives  

\[
\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\le kn+\frac{(n-k)(n+k+1)}{2}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
k\le n-2 .
\tag{8}
\]

Thus no configuration can contain more than \(n-2\) sunny lines.
For \(n=3,4\) the right‑hand side of (8) equals \(1\); for \(n\ge5\) it equals
\(n-2\).  Hence the maximal possible number of sunny lines is exactly the
quantity stated in the answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Constructions attaining every admissible \(k\)

Fix \(n\ge3\) and an integer \(k\) satisfying (8).

#### 3.1  Vertical backbone  

For each \(i=1,\dots ,n\) take the vertical line  

\[
L_i:\;x=i .
\]

These \(n\) lines are distinct, non‑sunny, and together they cover every
column \(C_i\), hence all of \(\mathcal P_n\).

#### 3.2  Replacing columns that consist of a single point  

The columns that contain exactly one point are  

\[
C_n=\{(n,1)\},
\qquad
\text{and, when }n\ge5,\;
C_{n-1}=\{(n-1,2)\}.
\]

Choose any \(k\) of these columns (possible precisely because of (8)).
For each chosen column \(C_i\) delete the vertical line \(L_i\) and insert the
sunny line  

\[
S_i:\; y-(n+1-i)=\frac12\bigl(x-i\bigr).
\]

The slope \(\tfrac12\) is different from \(0,\infty,-1\); therefore \(S_i\) is
sunny.  Because the line has a non‑vertical direction, the only lattice point
of \(\mathcal P_n\) lying on it is its defining point \((i,n+1-i)\).  Consequently
\(S_i\) covers exactly the unique point of the replaced column.

After performing the replacement for the selected \(k\) columns we have:

* exactly \(k\) sunny lines (\(S_i\));
* the remaining \(n-k\) vertical lines still cover all points of the untouched
  columns;
* the total number of lines remains \(n\).

Thus every integer \(k\) that satisfies (8) is realizable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

The upper‑bound argument shows that no configuration can have more than the
numbers of sunny lines listed in (8).  The explicit construction shows that each
value allowed by (8) is attainable.  Therefore the set of possible numbers of
sunny lines is exactly  

\[
\boxed{\begin{cases}
\{0,1\}, & n=3\text{ or }n=4,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,\dots ,n-2\}, & n\ge5 .
\end{cases}}
\]

∎
